utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case Number IT-02-60-T, The Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Today we'll continue the proceedings. But before that, there are several procedural matters I would like to address. The first one is that on the 15th of December, the Appeals Chamber dismissed before Vidoje Blagojevic's appeal of the Trial Chamber's decision concerning this Counsel issue. Accordingly, Mr. Karnavas and Mrs. Tomanovic will remain as Mr. Blagojevic's counsel. But that does not mean that there's no fault or problem on the part of the Defence team. If a lawyer could not win the confidence and the trust of his client, he's not a good lawyer, at least in my jurisdiction. So I hope Mr. Karnavas could take the initiative to approach to your client and rebuild the confidence and the trust. The reasons of that decision by the Appeals Chamber will follow and will be made available to Mr. Blagojevic in B/C/S as soon as practical thereafter. I want to stress here that the option for a legal representative remains available to Mr. Blagojevic if he wants that legal representative. This Trial Chamber has taken extraordinary measures to create that so-called legal representative to help Mr. Blagojevic help himself. I must confess in the Statute and the Rules of Evidence and Procedures, there's no such kind of legal representative. Another thing I want to mention, the specific mandate for the independent counsel as defined in the Trial Chamber's May 9th order has been fulfilled. If Mr. Blagojevic wants to have a better understanding of the reasons of the Appeals Chamber, he may first approach Mr. Karnavas. I believe that Mr. Karnavas will help him to understand the meanings of the reasoning of the Appeals Chamber. Secondly, he may use the legal representative assigned to him, and I am told that the Registrar is ready to provide a list for him to choose. The second issue is about the motion of Mr. Jokic related to disclosure of Rule 68 materials of the 15th September, 2003. Following the Prosecution's response of 17th December in which the Prosecution states that "all the material that Mr. Jokic's Defence has asked for has been previously provided to it." Does Mr. Jokic's Defence wish to withdraw this motion?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do not wish to withdraw the motion. But we are satisfied with the answer from the Prosecution has fulfilled their obligations under Rule 68. And that becomes part of the record, and we would like it to remain part of the record, that they have stated they have fulfilled their obligations. Which we trust that they have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. But if you do not withdraw this motion, I'm afraid that the Trial Chamber has to dismiss it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, I would like the motion to stay on file saying that we asked for it because it makes a record that we are continually putting the Prosecution to its burden of providing under Rule 68. And I think the next step would be that the Trial Chamber would have a finding that the Prosecution has satisfied that burden. But whatever the Court wishes to do, this Honourable Trial Chamber wishes to do with it, I would like it to stay on the record that we have requested that information that was used during Mr. Obrenovic's request for provisional release. And we're not so sure that we have it in our hands, but maybe we'll be able to locate it as soon as possible, with the help of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand your meaning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The third matter is the presence of Mr. Nikolic's counsel in the courtroom and his status. Today, we are going to hear a very material witness; that is, Mr. Nikolic, a former co-accused and a convicted person waiting sentencing in another case. He's testifying as a Prosecution witness. His presence here as a witness, and he still has proceedings pending before this Bench which may be affected by his testimony in this case. And as he has not waived his right to be represented by counsel in those proceedings, the Trial Chamber finds that it is appropriate for his counsel to be present in the courtroom throughout his testimony. The Trial Chamber would like to make it clear that the only parties to these proceedings are the Prosecution and the Defence for Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Jokic. It is these parties who will be examining Mr. Nikolic and have the right to address the Trial Chamber in relation to his examination or cross-examination. Mr. Nikolic may, however, ask to consult his counsel in the course of his testimony, and the Trial Chamber will grant him the opportunity for such consultation. Are there any other matters the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench? Yes, Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, having considered everything you've just said, I would like to point out three very important issues. The trial was in recess, and now I wish to say that I have no counsel representing and defending me in this case before this Tribunal. Secondly, I was visited at the Detention Unit yesterday by Mr. Rajlic, the infantry colonel retired. I hired Mr. Dragutin Ilic as my military expert on my Defence team. I wish to use his expertise on several military issues. Ilic told me that Mr. Karnavas had sent him to see me, and that he had brought him directly from Belgrade the day before. Therefore, Mr. Karnavas instructed Ilic to tell me that Mr. Ilic, who was visiting me, should sit here in the courtroom and listen to Nikolic's and Obrenovic's testimonies. And on the basis of that, to put together questions for cross-examination and give them to Mr. Karnavas in order for Mr. Karnavas to cross-examine Nikolic and Obrenovic. Furthermore, he told me that Mrs. Tomanovic saw him back to the gate of the Detention Unit encouraging him to succeed in his mission. For obvious reasons, I turned all of this down. I broke my meeting with Mr. Ilic in less than five minutes. I told Ilic that he was in no position to exercise that kind of work, that he was not competent for that kind of work, and this was far above his duties as part of our Defence team. I abide by my position that Mr. Ilic, as a military expert, may, based on his study of certain military documents, provide an expert analysis of maybe two or three very, very specialised military issues. It is my belief that the art of cross-examination is taught in special schools, and this duty cannot be taken over by a retired officer. These actions of Mr. Karnavas have only deepened the gulf between the two of us, and my mistrust of his behaviour and his work. And it further exacerbates my doubt concerning his work which will not be to my benefit as I believe, but rather detrimental to me. Thirdly, I would like to have again forwarded to me the decision of the Appeals Chamber containing the reasons and to have a meeting with Mr. Sekrun [phoen], an independent lawyer, who will then explain to me all the legal reasoning and qualifications from the brief version and the long, integral version of this decision of the Appeals Chamber. Your Honours, this is all I wish to say. Please try to understand why I have raised these three issues. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll respond to Mr. Blagojevic's concerns first, and then my other concerns. When I was retained by Mr. Blagojevic, I made it very clear that I would be selecting every member of the Defence team. In that process, I asked for him to give me recommendations of potential expert witnesses, military expert witnesses. After interviewing several of them, and after a period of approximately six months, we met -- I met with Professor Ilic, who is, in fact, one of the authors of the rules on brigade -- on the brigade rules for the VRS or for the JNA and has also taught at the military academy teaching generals how to become generals or colonels how to advance to the level of generals. Having been impressed by Mr. Ilic for, one, his knowledge, two, his professionalism, three, his objectivity, I brought him on to the team for a very few hours, though he has been working more or less full time on this case because of his commitment to the Defence. Mr. Ilic was brought to The Hague once before with another military expert and spent approximately three and a half days with Mr. Blagojevic, again going over all of the military matters. For my experience, having practiced 20 years as a trial lawyer, having taught trial advocacy, having taught how to cross-examine experts, it's my opinion that no lawyer can cross-examine an expert unless he or she becomes an expert themselves prior to the cross-examination and works with an expert, both in assisting in the cross-examination and setting up the direct examination for the Defence case. Mr. Ilic, or Professor Ilic has been assisting us in that capacity. Mr. Blagojevic is fully aware of that. Secondly, a few months ago, Mr. Blagojevic contacted Mr. Ilic in Belgrade and spoke to him over the phone asking him to remain on the team in the event the Karnavas/Tomanovic Defence team were to be dismissed, at which point, Professor Ilic indicated that he would remain as the expert in the case if Mr. Blagojevic so desired. It was Professor Ilic's understanding from the conversation that Mr. Blagojevic was reaching out and was -- to Mr. Ilic to assist. After receiving the final decision from the Court - and might I add, before the decision throughout while we have been in recess, we have been intensively working on the cross-examination of Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Obrenovic through our expert witnesses. We've met with Professor Ilic in Belgrade. I met with him with Ms. Tomanovic; Ms. Tomanovic met with him in addition on her own. So this is not something new. But in any event recognising now that the Prosecution has switched its list and was bringing Nikolic on forward, we went to great pains to rush Mr. Ilic over here, yes, to assist us, because after all he has spent his entire life in the military and I haven't. If I am going to provide the best possible legal assistance to Mr. Blagojevic, I need someone like that to assist me. So that was the reason. I also thought, given the Court's understanding that we should be reaching out to the client, and in light of the Court's earlier remarks which I do take some difference to, as to whether I'm a good lawyer or bad lawyer, I thought that this would be one more effort, and the cost of bringing Mr. Ilic over here for the next two or three years are being borne by the Defence team, not by the Registrar who will not pay for this sort of assistance. So it is an added cost to the Defence that we're willing, gladly, to have in order to provide Mr. Blagojevic with the best possible defence. And so it was decided that it would be best if Mr. Ilic could meet with Mr. Blagojevic and speak with him before Mr. Nikolic took the stand; one, to convoy the issues that we were planning, that we thought were relevant to the cross-examination; and two, to solicit any particular areas of concern Mr. Blagojevic may wish to have with respect to the cross-examination. And I want to stress that throughout this entire period, we have been sending letters repeatedly to Mr. Blagojevic seeking a meeting with him. However, he has refused to communicate. So it's not for lack of trying, and I don't know what else I can possibly do to win this gentleman's confidence at this stage of the game, which may be a reason for me to be withdrawn. I leave that to the Court and the Registrar. But nonetheless, we have been making these efforts. So that was the purpose for Mr. Ilic meeting with Mr. Blagojevic. Yes, we had hoped that the meeting would be successful. No, we are not that concerned that because of the lack of its success that we are unable to go forward. We are. So I'll leave it at that. The only other issue I wish to bring up at this point, Your Honour, was with respect to the last point that you raised with -- in regards to the lawyers for the witness, Mr. Nikolic. I understand he was a co-accused before. But now he is a witness. He has waived his right to remain silent. And I think it is very, very -- I cannot see -- I'm unaware of, I should say, I'm unaware of any legal precedence where a witness is allowed to consult with his lawyer in answering questions in the middle of a trial proceeding. And I take strong objection to that. I want to register my objection, not only to that but also to their presence. I understand they wish to be present because they need to make sure at the end that they can argue convincingly to the Court that their client has fully cooperated and has been truthful in his testimony. They can be provided -- first, they can watch as they're watching right now from the public gallery. Secondly, they can be provided with a full transcript of any of the closed proceedings. So they are not going to be prejudiced. But I do take exception to Mr. Nikolic being treated as a privileged VIP in the courtroom when he's nothing more than a witness at this point. And I understand he hasn't been sentenced yet, but nonetheless as a witness, I believe he should not be consulting his lawyers prior to answering questions. The only other area where I know this happens is in the United States in the grand jury proceedings where a witness is allowed to go outside the proceedings and consult with a lawyer. There may be other jurisdictions that allow this. I'm unaware of it. However, I do think for the process that we have before this International Criminal Tribunal, it is a dangerous precedent to set unless it has been set that I'm totally unaware of. And if it has been set and I'm unaware of it, then I still stand by my comments, but I apologise for my ignorance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me deal with these issues one by one. The first one is that Mr. Blagojevic claims that he is not represented by a lawyer. This Bench could not agree with you, especially after we received the decisions from the Appeals Chamber. I quite understand what you are thinking and what's in your mind after hearing the decisions from the Appeals Chamber. As you probably know that I'm a Trial Judge in Krnojelac's case, and the day before yesterday, the Appeals Chamber rendered a decision overruling almost all the findings of the Trial Chamber. But as for the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and in all other jurisdictions, the Appeals Chamber's decision has the binding force on the Trial Chamber and on everything. I promised you many times, I believe, that whatever conclusions the Appeals Chamber may arrive at, this Bench will comply with it. So I said at the very beginning, that Mr. Karnavas and Mrs. Tomanovic will remain as your counsel. There's no doubt about it, especially we received the decisions from the Appeals Chamber. Secondly, this Bench appreciates the effort by Mr. Karnavas to call a legal -- a military expert. We regard it as an effort from the Defence team to rebuild the confidence of his client. But after all, this is a matter between the lead counsel and his client. The Chamber has no mandate to interfere in this matter. I hope the two of you could find a way out to this issue because, as I said, we are going to hear a very material witness today and after today. As for the third matter Mr. Blagojevic mentioned, we believe his request is reasonable. He needs somebody to help him to understand the reasonings of the decisions of the Appeals Chamber. As for the functions of that independent counsel, I believe that we have to consult with the Registrar to see whether to explain the meaning of that decision is still within the mandate of that independent counsel. There's objections from the Defence team of Mr. Blagojevic the functions of the Defence team of Nikolic. Before making decision, this Bench also made some research into the jurisprudence this Tribunal. In other cases, in the same situation, the counsels for the witness were allowed to be present in the proceedings in this courtroom. And the witness has the right to consult with his counsel during the proceedings or during the break. Well, we have spent much more time than I expected in those procedural matters. Having said that, could we have the witness, please. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, good morning. We had one other procedural matter which if we could go into private session briefly after counsel and witness get here, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. If your matter is related towards certain documents, could we come to that when we come across that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, it was going to be the first thing I dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please stand up. Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could go into private session very briefly, then we'll be ready to get started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in open session. You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, good morning, could you state your full name, please, spell your last name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. McCloskey. My name is Momir Nikolic. M-o-m-i-r, N-i-k-o-l-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you have plead guilty to the persecutions indictment in this case. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I pleaded guilty on count 5 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you stand by that guilty plea and acknowledge your criminal responsibility in this case?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by my guilty plea with regard to count 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you enter into a plea agreement with the Prosecution in this case?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes, we entered into a plea agreement which I have signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you testifying today in part pursuant to that plea agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, because I'm obliged to do so according to the agreement. It is my duty to testify on the basis of that agreement within these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And within that agreement, there is a declaration that Mr. Karnavas has so kindly referred us to. And I would mark that as P81. During the discussions prior to your plea, did you make two false statements to the Prosecution taking responsibility for Kravica and falsely identifying yourself in a photograph?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Shortly after making those false statements, did you realise that was wrong?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I realised that I had made a mistake. I can state the reasons if the Trial Chamber would like me to do so. But I did realise that I had made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are those reasons in part spelled out in this document, the declaration P81?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, they have been spelled out in part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You made those false statements because you thought it would assist you in gaining a plea agreement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the leading nature of the -- you know, I did not object too much with the other witnesses. However, at this stage, with these witnesses, I'm going to ask Mr. McCloskey and his team to please not lead witnesses while they do their direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, you may ask why he made those false statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us why, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: With regard to the photograph, I initially said that I could recognise myself in the photograph. At that time, I was not sure because the person in the photograph really looks like me. The first photograph that I had was not very clear. It was a fairly bad photograph. And this is something that I also stated when I spoke to you, and I identified myself in that photograph because that's what I believed. I believed that to be a photograph depicting myself. Shortly after that, my lawyers investigated that matter, and the person was identified and a first and last name was given to that person in the photograph. So it was quite normal for me to say that the person in the photograph was, in fact, not myself. That's the explanation I have to give as far as the photograph is concerned. As far as the statement I made that is in the statement provided, I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that that was my decision, that was an assessment that I made. And at that time, I was not influenced by my lawyers or by the Prosecution. No one exercised any pressure on me at that time. No one exerted any pressure on me. Once the agreements with the Prosecution had already advanced, I came to the decision that there would be no agreement, and I really wanted to obtain an agreement. I made a mistake. I admitted something I hadn't done because I wanted to obtain such an agreement. I accepted responsibility for something that I had not done. I accepted a greater degree of responsibility. But when we met again, when I spoke to the Prosecution again, I first of all told my lawyers, and then Mr. McCloskey, that I had made a mistake, that I hadn't told the truth. I apologised for that. And I said that in the next interview, in our future discussions, I would attempt to tell the truth to the best of my recollection. And that is what happened. Those are the explanations I can provide with regard to these two matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you understand today and throughout the rest of your testimony how critically important it is for you to tell the whole truth?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you first tell us how old are you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1955. So I'm 48 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was born in Bratunac, in a village in the village of Hrancin in Bratunac on the 20th of February, 1955.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where did you grow up and go to your beginning schools?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I grew up in the village I was born in. I went to primary school in my municipality, the municipality of Bratunac. And likewise, I went to secondary school in Bratunac. It was a school for construction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you first get to know Mr. Blagojevic, your former commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Blagojevic and his family -- well, I had known them for my entire life. But we personally met when he came -- when he joined the army of Republika Srpska. And we became more familiar when he came to the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you see Mr. Blagojevic in court today?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you point him out to us, tell us what he's wearing.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic is sitting between the guard on the right, if you're looking from my direction, between Mr. Jokic and the guard. As far as I can see from here, he's wearing a light-coloured shirt. He has a dark suit, a grey suit. He's wearing a tie.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let the record reflect the witness has identified the defendant Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Tell us a little more about your schooling, what you studied, what occupation or profession you wanted to get into.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After I had completed secondary school, secondary technical school, after I had done my military service in the former JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, I did my military service in Slovenia. I spent 15 months there. After my military service had been completed, I enrolled in university to study political science. I studied the subject of defence and protection in 1977, 1977. I graduated in 1981, in February. On the 17th of February, 1981, that is when I graduated. So it took me three, three and a half years to graduate. I graduated a little early. Having graduated, I returned to the municipality of Bratunac. I got a job as a professor in the secondary school centre, Djuro Pucar Stari. I worked in that secondary school centre until 1986. And after that, I moved over to the Territorial Defence staff where I worked as assistant commander for intelligence. While I was performing those duties, the war broke out. I was mobilised on the 18th of April. I was mobilised into the Territorial Defence, like many other people from Bratunac. And during that crisis period, from about the 25th of April, I acted as commander of the Territorial Defence staff in Bratunac. I had never been appointed to that post by an order or by a document issued by a superior command. After that, I spent a certain period of time in Serbia. I can tell you the reasons for having spent some time there if the Trial Chamber is interested in them. I returned in November, sometime in November 1992. And after a week, I was assigned to the post of assistant commander for security and intelligence in the Bratunac Brigade. I remained at that post in the Bratunac Brigade until the end of the war. After the end of the war and demobilisation on the 20th of April, 1996, I was appointed as chief of the department of the ministry for refugees and displaced persons in Bratunac and as coordinator of that ministry for the municipality of Srebrenica. I remained in that ministry for 15 months. After that, I was appointed as director in the municipality of Bratunac, I was appointed as director of the international company Guber in Bratunac. After the multiparty elections were held, I was replaced because that post was taken by the SDS, or rather by the radical party and the SDS party. I was unemployed for one year after that. And then after a year at the assembly, I was again appointed as director of the Kartonaza Bratunac company. I remained there until privatisation occurred, and after the privatisation had been carried out, I was unemployed again, and that was the period during which I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, thank you for that biographical background. For the biographical background, that was fine, but now we need to go question by question now. Okay? Now, you remained the chief of intelligence and security for the Bratunac Brigade. The period of spring up to July 1995, can you describe to us briefly the structure of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, just briefly. How was it different than a regular infantry brigade? How many battalions, for example?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: There were three infantry battalions in the Bratunac Brigade, as per establishment as far as I know. And if we're talking about this critical period, then there was a battalion from the Zvornik Brigade which was attached to the Bratunac Brigade, but it didn't form part of its composition. The Bratunac Brigade had its command in -- there was a commander in the command of the Bratunac Brigade, and then there was a chief of staff, an assistant commander for morale, religious and moral guidance, assistant commander for logistics. There was a chief of the security and intelligence organ. And I'm not sure whether it was the assistant of the commander or the chief of staff of mobilisation and personnel affairs. In addition to those units, rather commands of the battalion, the Bratunac Brigade had a military police platoon. According to establishment, it had a reconnaissance platoon. It had a mixed artillery battery. It had a logistics platoon. Perhaps I have forgotten to mention something, but on the whole that would be its composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And about how many men under arms did it have in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I really couldn't provide you with precise information for the battalions, but a battalion has between 450 and 500 men, according to establishment. It was never brought up to strength in accordance with the establishment, but if there were about three battalions, that would be about 1.500 men. Perhaps there were another 300 or 400 men in other units and commands. So I'm not sure exactly how many men there were, but about 1.800 men, up to 2.000 men, if you include the 4th Battalion which was attached to the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About what date roughly, as you recall, did Colonel Blagojevic come over and take over command of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think Colonel Blagojevic came in a direct manner before the Srebrenica operation. I'm not sure whether that was in April or May. I really don't know the exact date of his arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had he been in that brigade in any capacity prior to that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. At one time, he was the chief of staff of the Bratunac Brigade when Colonel Jovanovic was the commander of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that -- could you pronounce the name of that other colonel for the booth, the former commander.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The name of the former commander was Slavko Ognjenovic, and I think that Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic was the chief of staff at that time, the chief of staff in the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What year roughly, or what time period?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think that was in 1994. I really don't know the exact period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in July 1995, who was the chief of staff deputy commander for the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The chief of staff, and at the same time, the deputy commander was Major Novica Pajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was the next person in rank of hierarchy of authority, after Mr. Pajic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After Mr. Pajic, there were the assistant commanders. All I can say now is what I believe. I did not see any official lists indicating who came after him, but that could perhaps be the assistant commander for logistics, the assistant commander for moral, religious -- and religious guidance. Perhaps the assistant commander for organisational affairs and personnel, and then the chief of the security and intelligence organ in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you name the individuals whose positions you just described.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, the assistant commander for the Bratunac Brigade was reserve Major Trisic, Dragoslav. The assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs was also the reserve major Jeftic, Ratko. The assistant or the deputy commander of the staff for organisation, mobilisation and personnel affairs was the active-duty officer Major Dragomir Eskic, and the chief of the organ for security and intelligence, I was that person, reserve captain Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've made a difference between active-duty officers and reserve officers. Could you explain that to the Court, what that difference is.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I'll try to do so. Active-duty officers are professional soldiers who have been schooled for such posts in military units, whereas reserve officers are people who have other professions. These people are usually people who have finished schools for reserve officers. That's what such schools were called among civilians. In peacetime, these people had other jobs. They weren't involved in the military profession. That wasn't their job. But when there's an imminent danger of war and in the course of war, these reserve officers are mobilised and join units. They're assigned to units. That would be the main difference between reserve officers and active-duty officers. There are certainly other differences, too, but those are the main ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there a difference in how much they got paid and where they got paid from?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that there was a difference in the way they were paid, a difference in the salaries of reserve officers and active-duty officers. Active-duty officers received their monthly salaries from the JNA budget. I think that their rights were regulated, their rights and other status issued. They were regulated through the 30th personnel centre which was located in Belgrade, whereas reserve officers received salaries from funds that formed part of the budget of Republika Srpska. That is what is most likely. That was one of the differences. And then another difference was that, for example, in respect of the same position, same rank, the income of a reserve officer and an active-duty officer would differ, even though they held the same rank and same position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. In July 1995, how many soldiers were in the military police battalion -- platoon of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In July, the military police battalion had 30 military policemen. There were 3 squads and 1 platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the command structure of the military police platoon.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The military police platoon had three squads. In each squad, there were nine policemen, plus the commander. Three squads would form a platoon. Within the platoon, there was the commander of the military police platoon and his deputy. This military police squad -- this military police platoon didn't have particular squads, for example, for transport, traffic, et cetera. The structure was very simple. It was the simplest structure that a military police platoon could have. And its purpose was to carry out usual military police duties and fulfill the needs of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the military police platoon?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The commander of the military police platoon, that was Mirko Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was his rank?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think he did not hold a military rank. He was a former active-duty policeman working in Tuzla. After the war broke out, he came back to Bratunac where he had been born, and then he joined the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was his immediate commander? Who was Mirko Jankovic's immediate commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: His immediate commander, meaning the one issuing orders to Mirko Jankovic and the military police platoon was the brigade commander. In this particular case, Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe what the normal duties of the military police were engaged in before the attack on the enclave on July 6th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Mainly, the military police platoon was carrying out tasks within the purview of all the usual military and police tasks. This entailed duties on the bridge over the Drina River, providing security for the gate at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters. They also had tasks at the Zuti Most yellow bridge checkpoint, and most of the time they would bring in military conscripts who went absent without official leave from their units, without authorisation from their commanders. They provide security whenever necessary for the brigade commanders, commanders and officers -- other commanders and other officers as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe where the checkpoint of yellow bridge or Zuti Most is for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Certainly, the yellow bridge checkpoint straddles the road between Bratunac towards Srebrenica. The distance may be, roughly speaking, 3 or 3 and a half kilometres from the centre of the town of Bratunac in the direction of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Going back to Mr. Trisic, can you describe his position and what his general duties were.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. -- That is Major Trisic was assistant commander for logistics. Mainly and briefly, his task was to look after the brigade's logistics, to provide everything that the brigade needs, to provide all the logistic support and the supplies needed. First and foremost, the materiel and technical equipment, and then all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's now go to your position, as you've described, as the chief of intelligence and security for the brigade. Is that a combined position, as it sounds, intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In other brigades, is this position always combined like this?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was the same thing in all the Light Infantry brigades. Infantry brigades, on the other hand, were different. In all infantry brigades, these two were separate positions or duties, whereas in light infantry brigades, the intelligence and security affairs were joined and this duty would usually be carried out by a single person, official.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in the Drina Corps, the organisation above the brigades, how were intelligence and security organised? Just briefly, were they combined or separate?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The Drina Corps as such had a department for intelligence and security. As far as I know, the Drina Corps kept those two positions separate. They had on the one hand chief of intelligence and on the other hand the chief of security. However, as far as I know - I'm not sure about this, however - the commander, or rather the chief of the intelligence department was also the chief of security, and that was Vujadin Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, I've --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, I hit the wrong button.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So who was the chief of intelligence of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The chief of intelligence of the Drina Corps was Lieutenant-colonel Vujadin Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was that chief of intelligence or security, Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He was the chief of security in the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was the chief of intelligence in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Briefly go back, you described that there is a combination of intelligence and security in light infantry brigades. What other basic differences are there between a light infantry brigade and a regular infantry brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, in addition to the number of units and their size, and what I've spoken about in relation to security and intelligence, I think the internal organisation of these different brigades were alike. I know about my own sector. I know that the infantry brigades were keeping those positions separate, as far as my sector is concerned. And I know that this particular position was a concurrent position in a light infantry brigade. I never studied in depth the structure of the infantry brigade, but this is one difference that I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe for us your duties, especially in 1995, prior to the attack on the Srebrenica enclave. What were your duties, and let's first concentrate on intelligence. And then I'll ask you about security, and you can tell us how they interacted.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How they interacted, do you mean the intelligence part of my operations and the security part of my operations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, first tell us what you as an intelligence officer did, what was your basic job.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My fundamental tasks as concerned intelligence activities were mostly related to gathering, monitoring, and processing information, operative information, on the enemy. Monitoring all the activities, assessing the strength, equipment, and weapons at the enemy's disposal, analysing their movements and their intentions. Everything that concerned the enemy. In this case, in 1995, the enemy we were talking about were the Muslim forces. As for security-related issues, mostly it was about planning and proposing security measures in order to protect our own forces, our own units, to protect our weapons, our equipment, and everything else that could have been attacked by the enemy as part of a military operation or outside any operations. To put it simply, those were intelligence and security tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who did you -- who was your immediate supervisor? Who did you report to as the chief of intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The immediate supervisor, my immediate supervisor would have been the brigade commander, and my superior, my direct superior was the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in July of 1995, that was Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Blagojevic was at that time the brigade commander, my superior, as well as the superior commander of all the other assistant commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was your relationship and your duties in relation to the military police platoon?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As for the military police platoon, I was in charge of expert coordination of the military police platoon. This means that I was responsible for the combat readiness of that particular unit and for training the unit of the military police platoon, training them to carry out military police tasks and any other tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have -- was it your job to propose uses of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. As for that aspect, my task was to propose to the commander the most economical way to use the military police in carrying out missions, missions potentially defined by the commander himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If the commander accepts your proposal for the use of the military police, what would your duties be in a normal situation to see that that proposal was carried out?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If the commander accepts my proposal concerning the carrying out of a mission, then I would make an assessment, I would instruct the military police commander if I deemed it necessary. If the tasks were of a more general police, military nature, I would just inform the military police platoon commander about the task. If this task was given at a meeting or at a briefing where commanders were present, and the commander of the military police platoon was not, I would just convey this order to him, this task. I would monitor their effort, and I would make sure that it was carried out as ordered by the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us some examples of how practically this worked in the everyday workings prior to the Srebrenica event.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, for instance, here's an example: Bringing in military conscripts who went absent without leave from their units. This is how it worked. Battalion commanders would report those missing without authorisation from their units. A list would be drawn up and forwarded to the commander of the military police platoon. Depending on how many people were missing from the unit or from the units, then there would be a briefing with the commander present. As this was a day-to-day task, I would make a proposal as to what to do. And I would forward this proposal to the commander, I would propose how many military policemen I thought were needed to carry out this task. The commander would then accept my proposal, or propose other measures himself, something that he thought was priority, a priority task. He'd listen to my proposal and the proposals of other assistant commanders concerning other issues following which he would make decisions and define tasks. More specifically, the tasks to be carried out by the military policemen. I would convey this defined task to the commander unless he was already present at the briefing. And then accordingly, that is, in keeping with the orders given by the commander, we would try hard to carry out this order in a timely fashion and exactly as ordered. Whatever aspects were not clear, professionally speaking, it was up to me to explain everything to the commander of the military police, to instruct him how to go about this particular task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What kind of discretion and trust did your commander have in you to do these duties in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, my commander should speak about this. But in view of the relationships then in town, I think there was a sufficient measure of trust as concerns my own responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he ever relinquish his power of command of the military police over to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. And we started late this morning for 30 minutes because of the technical problems. But since we have a large presence in this room, that is more than 25 people, I have been asked to guarantee that the break will be 30 minutes. So we'll resume at quarter past 11.00. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know when we will finish, the regular time, or will we go a little longer to make up for it? Just for planning purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I have to consult with the Registrar about it. So the hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, during the break, I had an opportunity to consult with Madam Registrar, and she is kind enough to allow us to sit 30 minutes more, which means that we'll break at 2.15 to make up the 30 minutes we lost at the beginning. Yes, Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, referring to your intelligence duties, as you have briefly described them, who did you report to regarding intelligence information and duties? Who was your immediate supervisor for intelligence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior for this in Bratunac Brigade and for other tasks was the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to look on the screen if you could to what is the Prosecutor's Exhibit 84B. That's the B/C/S. And I don't want to go into the detail of this, but this is from a book dated from 1984 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, would you please wait a minute. We have some problems here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that. Mr. McCloskey, you may start.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But we also have a problem with this document because it's not that clear on the screen. Do you have some hard copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Mr. President. I've got three screens, and it's a different clarity on each one. So we've asked them to have the ELMO ready in this event, so we can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, can you -- if you could take a look at this first page. I don't know if your screen is readable, but the document next to you certainly is readable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may object to it --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If Mr. McCloskey could just properly introduce the document, identify it for the record, that it has been marked for identification, and just do it in a proper fashion as opposed to launching right in and asking the witness to identify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, that may be a good idea. Mr. McCloskey, would you please make some foundations for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, as I referred to before the break, this is a B/C/S document, Prosecutor's 84B. And if the witness could look at this document and identify it for us if he can. In fact, we have the complete document which has been provided to everyone, and that may be easier for him as opposed to a page inside the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be of some assistance here, and I don't wish to interrupt the Prosecutor. However, this is one page from a particular document. If you could just identify the document itself, the entire document, introduce the document perhaps, and then get to the page itself because having one page out of a text which is where this comes from makes it very difficult for the rest of the text to come in at this point in time, which is necessary under the rule of completeness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's what we're doing, I think. I have now asked Mr. Nikolic to look at the complete document, which is B/C/S 84B. He now has that in front of him. And it's because we don't have enough screens, I can tell the Court of this document in English is "Rules of service of security organs in the armed forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia," dated 1984. And we will have an English version of that also marked as 84A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, does this -- does this document, is it all familiar to you? Can you identify what it is?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This document I have in front of me is an instruction concerning the methods and -- used in the work of the security organs of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does that -- did that book have any relevance to you in your work as a VRS officer throughout the wartime period?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part, as concerns the rules and this document, I used this book of rules and this particular rule in my work, in exercising my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you use any other manual for -- of rules related to your security work?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In connection with my duties as a security officer, I mostly used these instructions concerning the work of the JNA, and I had no other instructions or documents. I did occasionally use another set of instructions, but this was related not to security affairs, but rather intelligence affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what instructions you used for intelligence affairs, if you could name the book and the date, if you know it.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: For intelligence affairs, I used a manual entitled "Intelligence Security for Combat Operations," which was published in 1987. This is a manual that I used when I worked for the Territorial Defence staff, and also after that I was using the same manual when I worked for the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may interrupt here again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I notice that the witness is looking down. I don't know if he's looking at any prepared notes that he has. I noticed that when he did walk in he came in with some notes in his hand. I would ask that he not refer to any notes unless he needs to refresh his recollection. So I don't know, and I'm not suggesting that he is looking, but I've noticed it. I am concerned. I would like to make sure that he's testifying independently from his memory. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, do you know about this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm a little closer than Mr. Karnavas, and he's looking at the document I gave him. But he does have a stack of material in front of him, and he has never made a reference to it. But as a witness, I don't see any problem of him referring to something as long as he tells us what it is and he gives people a chance to look at it. I don't know what his plans are, Your Honour, regarding that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nikolic, do you have any notes at your hands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have here in front of me my own notes. You can have a look if like, but they are not at all related to this specific question. There is nothing here related to the question Mr. McCloskey asked. These notes are merely to refresh my memory. I used these notes when preparing my testimony as concerns this document. You can have a look if you like, and there is nothing in it about the document I have been speaking about. And if I may please explain something in relation to this document, to this rule --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question: You mean that you prepared this document yourself, rather than furnished by others. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your question, but which document exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I mean the note you have in your hands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, the notes. I prepared them on my own, and I was not receiving anyone else's instructions. I prepared this document in my own room, in my own cell at the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If the gentleman going to be referring to his notes, even though they are his notes, he's making reference to something that is not part of the record, I would ask that we be provided with a copy of his notes. I'm sure he would not object since obviously he's here to tell the truth and what is contained on the notes should be nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I agree with you. Mr. Nikolic, would you please give your notes to the Madam Registrar and ask --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- And pass them to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There has been no reference made to these notes in Court today. And as his private notes, until that happened, I don't see the relevance of that. I have no idea what's in them, except they are his private notes. Now, if they were made at the time of the events or something like that, I can see their relevance. But preparing -- notes that witness's prepare themselves for evidence, unless they are referred to in some way, they really should not be part of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, you know, I think you would like to have the testimony of this witness established on a sound basis so that it is the job of this Bench to ensure that there's nothing irregular. The purpose to let Defence counsel have a look of these notes is to erase their suspicions on this matter. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not sure we'll ever erase their suspicions, Your Honour, but I understand your ruling. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, if we're ready to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, let's -- can you tell us a bit more about this rules of service. It's dated 1984. What was it originally designed for, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mostly all the rules, including those concerning security organs, were meant to govern the work and the proper functioning, as well as the carrying out of tasks from the security and intelligence areas. The aim was to define the relationships within certain commands and certain units belonging to certain institutions, to define methods and means used by a security organ in its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For what institution was this book designed? What military organisation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This book was for military units, for military commands, institutions, initially for the staffs. Then for the brigade commands, corps commands, and even superior units and commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For which country?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The former Yugoslavia, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we know that in 1995, it was the entity or country of Republika Srpska. Did the army of the Republika Srpska have its own manuals for security and intelligence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the army of Republika Srpska did not publish any particular sets of instructions, rules. And I know, I am speaking from experience, that I myself used rules that had been used previously in the Yugoslav People's Army. Maybe there were some other sets of rules, but I was not using any other sets of rules. However, I cannot rule out the possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want you to explain for us, if you could, how your reporting procedures worked, both for intelligence and security. How would you communicate information to your command, first of all, and how would you communicate information to superior commands?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As for conveying intelligence information to my command, mostly this was done directly by speaking to them. And as a rule, this was done orally. All the intelligence gathered by using a variety of methods used in gathering information was conveyed to the command and the commander personally at meetings or outside meetings, depending on the grade of urgency pertaining to a particular piece of information. You sent written reports to a superior command, and a superior command would be informed in writing about the intelligence gathered. This was the usual method.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you communicated by writing to a superior command, what superior command are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I am talking about the Drina Corps command, the department for intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you normally communicate to the Drina Corps command about intelligence, or how did that work?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This worked very much in keeping with the relevant norms on a regular basis and whenever this was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These written documents to the Drina Corps, reports on intelligence, can you describe to us whose offices they went through, if any, before going to the corps. How they were transported, who got to see them.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'll answer your first question first. Those were written reports. Before they were forwarded to the Drina Corps command as reports, the command and the brigade commander were familiarised with the content of these reports. After that, I was the one who wrote those reports. They went to the communications centre, and then they would be coded at the communications centre, and they were sent off to the corps commander, rather, the department for security and intelligence affairs of the corps in a coded form.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So after you actually wrote the report down, did your command or anyone in the brigade look at it before you sent it off to intel and security, normally?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This did happen occasionally. I can only tell you that this was not the established practice, for every document to be looked at physically. But the established practice was to have the report shown to the commander and the brigade commander brigade commander and the brigade command, or rather the officers for whom this would have been relevant. This is in keeping with the rule governing intelligence work and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you're -- are you saying most of the time, the actual report, written report, did not go to your commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The written report would normally not go to the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But would you discuss -- generally discuss the contents of such reports prior to that report being sent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I know it doesn't sound it, but there's a leading nature to all of these questions, especially any question that begins with the word "so." It's a common knowledge that it's either a conclusiory [sic] or leading nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to these talking objections. This is the necessary argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you have to be patient. Let Mr. Karnavas finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What I am suggesting here is that the Prosecutor here, who has over twenty years of experience, should be asking non-leading questions on direct examination. This is a critical witness. We are not into a crime-based witness, so I would please ask that he ask non-leading questions, who, what, why, where, how, and explain, and I think we'll get along just fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, in this matter, I'm afraid I cannot agree with you. I checked all the questions starting with "so," and I don't see any leading natures. You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, we were trying to clarify whether or not it was the normal practice that you verbally informed your commander of the intelligence information, and then would send the written report without him reviewing it. Is that basically what you have been saying?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about intelligence information that you receive. Can you describe for us how you receive information from within your brigade, where you normally get it from and...

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Intelligence within the brigade would mostly come from subordinate units, from battalions, through battalion assistant commanders for security and intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, for security information and reports, is the process any different? If so, can you explain it.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question. I'm not quite sure which reports you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I will. And I apologise. When you -- can you describe to us the process by which you go through when you send a written security report to the intelligence and security unit of the corps. Is it any different than you've described for intelligence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The procedure is identical. It's quite the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you receive -- do you occasionally receive security information from the corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you describe how that normally works, how the information comes in, where it comes in.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If it concerns data information from a subordinate command, from the superior command, it came through the communications centre. It was coded. All documents on the whole would then be forwarded to the command. They would be placed on his desk. The commander would then familiarise himself with the documents that had arrived. He would direct the document to the addressee, the logistics organ, the personnel organ, the security organ, for example. Each assistant had his own number, Mil 1, Mil 2, 3, 4, 5, et cetera. Afterwards, it would go to an office where those documents were kept. And the clerk employed in that office gave those documents to the officers who were concerned by those documents, and the book would be personally signed. That was the usual procedure. Those were the rules that were followed when receiving posts and all documents in the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there any special procedures for security information?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, the procedure is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did the security branch from the corps have the right to send sealed information to the security officer, to the brigade, without the brigade commander seeing it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, such a right did exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why was that, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But I think that this was the exception rather than the rule. Sealed documents, information requests under seal addressed to the chief of security, well, this would happen only in cases when the request was addressed to the security organ and concerned, let's say, one of the officers from the Bratunac Brigade command, or perhaps if it concerned the commander of the unit who was suspected of having committed a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did the security officer of the brigade have the power to investigate his commander, if so ordered from above?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He had the power to carry out investigations and inform the superior command and the corps commander about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For information coming from the corps regarding intelligence, did the same procedures apply? Did the corps intelligence branch have the authority to send you sealed documents that your commander could not see?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. All intelligence was sent openly. It wasn't under seal. I never received intelligence that was under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And from July 1995 through November 1995, do you recall receiving any sealed information from the corps or the main staff, security information?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. I never received such information from the security organ or from the main staff. I never received such information that was under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other sort of special differences or privileges that security officers, that you yourself as a brigade chief of security, had aside from this ability to receive sealed mail?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I didn't have privileges of any kind, none at all, not with regard to any matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps "privileges" is the wrong word. Were there any procedures that you didn't have to go through that other officers might have to go through, in transportation or reporting to a military post or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, the security organs had the privilege of not having to be disarmed and detained in front of gates. It was sufficient for us to present ourselves, to show our papers. That's the only privilege I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in the Bratunac Brigade prior to the attack on the enclave on 6 July, 1995, was there any effort to begin an intelligence branch in the Bratunac Brigade, a separate intelligence branch as functioned in a normal brigade, as opposed to a light infantry brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If you're thinking about a separation of functions, if that's what you're referring to, in that case, my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you explain that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Sometime around April -- I'm not sure about this, but I think that the establishment, the brigade's establishment, was modified. And according to the new establishment, there was a post for the chief for intelligence. And at that point, there was a separation made -- a separation of duties. There was a chief of security and a chief of intelligence in the Bratunac Brigade. That was around the beginning of April, the 3rd or the 4th, in the year 1995. Dragisa Jovanovic was appointed as the assistant of the chief of staff for intelligence. And I'd just like to point out that Dragisa Jovanovic, up until the time he had been appointed to that post, was an officer for intelligence in the security and intelligence organ of the Bratunac Brigade. And that is, in fact, what was done in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, was that creation actually carried out?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In theory, yes. In terms of administrative procedure, yes, it was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What happened in practice, on the practical level?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, in practice, because of a number of circumstances that prevailed during that period, nothing of importance changed as far as the functioning of this organ is concerned. I remained the chief of that organ. All reports continued to be forwarded through me. Orders and information from the superior commander continued to be addressed to me. So in principle, nothing really changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Because Mr. Dragisa Jovanovic was absent at that time. He went to Trnovo. And he wasn't an educated man. He hadn't been trained to perform such duties on an independent basis. And if we're talking about that critical period, he wasn't prepared, and he was physically absent from the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "critical period," you mean from the time of the attack on the enclave until after, let's say, July 20th? What do you refer as you say, "the critical period"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, it's a minor point. But there's a way of asking the question in a non-leading fashion. What do you mean by critical point. He can explain. But by asking him and then giving him the answer, the suggested answer, is a leading manner --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree, and I cleaned it up at the end. This is silliness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, I don't want the Counsels to argue with each other directly. Well, in this matter, I agree with Mr. Karnavas. You have to rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's the critical point? What are the critical days?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: From about the beginning of the attack on the Srebrenica enclave, up until the 20th or the 22nd or the 23rd of July, 1995. Perhaps the period was a little longer. I really don't know exactly, but on the whole that would be the period concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know roughly when Mr. Jovanovic was able to go to the intelligence school to be trained?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I really don't know when he went to the school. I know that he was sent to Banja Luka. But as to the date, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When, if ever, did the separate intelligence organ get off its feet and actually start working?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't answer this question precisely as to when the intelligence organ came to life. He was appointed. He was trained. So in principle, the answer could be yes, because in practical and in theoretical terms it did exist as an organ. But there are always obstacles for it to function within the context of the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did it get functioning sometime after the fall of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just give us a rough estimate of, you know, how many months, weeks, days, whatever?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, let's say after return from Banja Luka, it was possible for something to be done independently, perhaps 15 or 20 days later. But I helped him with regard to this matter. And in fact, I continued performing such duties. I provided him with professional assistance, instructions. But he had to accept the decision because it was a definitive decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to the period of late 1994, early 1995. Can you describe the situation regarding the Srebrenica enclave. And I'll ask some particular questions. First, was the enclave demilitarised from the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I sent reports, and that was the assessment of the representative of the Serbian army. The assessment was that the demilitarisation in the Srebrenica enclave was not complete, and that was the assessment that was made at all levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me broaden my time frame to include all of 1995 up until the fall of the enclave. Can you describe what kind of Muslim military activities were carried out from within inside the enclave against Serb forces or civilians.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After Srebrenica had proclaimed to be a UN safe haven, and up until its fall, on the whole, ambushes were laid. There were attacks against positions of the units of the army of Republika Srpska, which were around the enclave. Sniper fire was opened at the positions of men outside the enclave. Attacks were carried out against certain villages or parts of villages that were on the border of the enclave. And other provocations were carried out. There were armed provocations from the enclave directed at the positions and units of the Bratunac Brigade and other brigades that surrounded the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what were -- what military activities, if any, were conducted by the VRS towards the inhabitants of the Srebrenica enclave in the time period from the beginning of the enclave through the beginning of the attack on Srebrenica?
