utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After Srebrenica had been proclaimed a protected zone on the 18th of April, 1994, the VRS units - I can talk about the units of the Bratunac Brigade in particular - they also opened sniper fire from their positions. They fired at members of the army and civilians in the enclave. And during that period, the units of the Bratunac Brigade on two occasions entered the demilitarised zone, and on one occasion, that was in the zone of responsibility of the 1st infantry battalion, and on the second occasion it was the responsibility of the 3rd infantry battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did the brigade commander at the time, Ognjenovic, ever made a policy statements regarding his intentions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I ask what the relevance is of all this. We don't have Mr. Ognjenovic here on trial. This period is not in the period of the indictment. So what the particular commander of the Bratunac Brigade policy was at that particular time prior to Mr. Blagojevic taking over the Bratunac Brigade, in my opinion, is not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, you have to lay some foundations for this question. Try to establish the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know, if you can answer briefly, how it happened that Muslims from all over Eastern Bosnia ended up in the Srebrenica enclave in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He needs to lay a foundation, and he can't do that through this particular witness. The way the question is phrased, it's as if somehow at the end of July or in July 1995, all of a sudden something happened. Srebrenica was an ongoing event. We all know that. The whole purpose of my objection was he's referring to a policy by a different commander that has nothing to do with Colonel Blagojevic. And that's why I objected on the grounds of relevancy. Now if Mr. McCloskey wishes to give us a proffer as to why he believes this area is relevant, then perhaps I might respond, and the Bench could make a ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you know, sometimes things don't happen at one time. There must be some process. I believe that Mr. McCloskey is trying to start from the very beginning of the process. And I believe that there is a consistent policy in that brigade, no matter who is the commander of that unit. And this Bench is eager to hear all those background informations before the enclave falls and before some incidents happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. However, with all due respect, and I say with this the utmost respect, as far as the continuity and policy, as far as I'm aware of, we haven't heard any particular evidence to lead me to believe there is a continuity in policy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I believe that this is the Prosecution's position and allegations. You may not agree with it, but you have the full opportunity to challenge it during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I briefly explain the foundational relevance of this question, just it may clear up things. I can go on, but it may help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think this is the first question I asked you, but you changed to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I misunderstood, Your Honours. I thought you wanted me to go through the witness for that information. As Your Honours are aware, the indictment outlines the events from the outbreak of the war and the -- what we have referred to as the cleansing of the Eastern Bosnia that resulted in many of the Muslims living in the Srebrenica safe area. We have outlined the two, three critical documents and actually placed them in the indictment that show this. There are several excellent reports, UN reports, that we have marked as exhibits that will outline this area. It's not an area I would prefer to go into great detail with this witness. The most relevant matter to this case is, as you're aware, the 1995 period, but a fundamental understanding of those basic time frames and those basic documents are important to understand what was going on when the enclave was attacked and fell. And so I -- my questions are relating to the 1994 period and the policy of the Bratunac Brigade command at that time, and I will continue if so allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, were you aware of a particular policy or statement of intent towards the enclave by the commander Ognjenovic in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. I was aware of a report of Mr. Ognjenovic's from 1994. And among other things, one of the positions it contained concerned the Srebrenica enclave, or rather, the relation towards the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was the position professed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In addition to a number of other issues included in this report, the report also stated the following: All activities and measures should be taken in regard of Srebrenica that would bring life in Srebrenica to a boiling point for its civilian population with the final and ultimate aim to get those people, the civilians, out of the enclave. This, of course, is a paraphrase of the original wording of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could ask the witness to look at Exhibit -- I'm sorry, I don't have an exhibit number yet, Mr. President. And we will get back to that when we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you could take a look at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I just want to ask whether everybody is furnished with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Everyone has had this for a very long time, and most recently it was given to everyone in a packet of material in the last couple of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This also is quoted in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, this document dated 4 July, 1994, by Commander Slavko Ognjenovic, does this appear to be the document you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any entitles for this document? You may read it so we could find it easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. "Report for the Brigade."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could direct your attention to the end of what's marked as paragraph 2, and is this the sentence you're referring to, and I'll quote: "The enemy's life has to be made unbearable, and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible realising that they cannot survive there"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was this statement made in any other way than this -- than in this particular document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I'd just like to make a correction related to the interpretation. This is a report meant to be looked at by brigade members. This is a report for brigade members written and signed by the then commander, Slavko Ognjenovic. I can only add that in this period of time, in 1994, I had no occasion to see any similar written documents in the Bratunac Brigade. Later, though, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was this document distributed to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: First of all, the Bratunac Brigade command was familiarised with this report at a meeting, a briefing. Further, this report was forwarded in its entirety to commanders of the subordinate units, battalion commanders, whose duty was to inform their units, all the officers and soldiers within their battalion, with the content of this report. As far as I knew, this was done, carried out in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When Mr. Blagojevic took over in the spring of 1995, did you see anything -- did he do anything to change this practice or to enforce this particular policy?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I want to object on the basis that no foundation has been laid with this particular witness. In other words, first, does the witness know if Mr. Blagojevic was, in fact, aware of this particular memorandum that was prepared by his predecessor? Then, the following -- the question asked by Mr. McCloskey would be proper. In other words, no foundation has been laid to ensure that this particular witness knows that Mr. Blagojevic at the time they took command over the Bratunac Brigade was aware of this particular policy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, you may ask the first question, whether the witness knows or not if Mr. Blagojevic was aware of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Blagojevic was aware of this document or this policy towards the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I really can't answer that question with any degree of accuracy. If at that time he was chief of staff of the Bratunac Brigade, which right now I cannot confirm because I simply don't know, then he must have been informed. If at that time when Ognjenovic was there, he was not the chief of staff, then I really can't say whether he knew about this or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: After he took over command, are you aware of any attacks on civilians in the enclave prior to the 6 July attack?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I've already answered this when answering your previous question. With regard to the entire period, as well as when Commander Blagojevic was there, fire was being opened on the enclave, on the civilians there, on the soldiers inside the enclave. This was a violation of the truce, and the arrival of another commander changed nothing in this respect. This was a permanent thing going on all the time. It was continuous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe what you mean in more detail what was continuous, these attacks on civilians and soldiers. Just tell us what you mean in particular.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As I was a communications officer, a liaison officer, I was in direct contact with the UN battalion based in Potocari. I was in touch with them constantly, talking to them and receiving their comments. They said fire was most usually coming from the positions of the 2nd infantry battalion and that they were firing at the people who lived just in front of those same positions. There were objections that the same thing was being done from the zone of responsibility of the 3rd infantry battalion, firing against people who were mowing their lawns and going about their daily business. I was always informed about these incidents. I was always receiving warnings from members of the Dutch Battalion, DutchBat, which spent most of the time in the enclave. I had personal knowledge that measures had been taken against perpetrators. I personally insisted that this be stopped, that we try to keep up the truce as it had been agreed, and I was, to a degree, successful in this. I can also tell you that following this report and in the period after that, the brigade members were encouraged by this. They saw that they could keep on opening fire at will and act in an irresponsible way in relation to the enclave itself and its population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there anything done by the Bratunac Brigade command to reduce the amount of international aid and convoys into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. As for convoys, I'll try to explain the situation. I was personally responsible for checks at the yellow bridge. I was personally responsible for everything concerning the entry of convoys, catering to the needs of DutchBat and the Muslim population. I'm talking about humanitarian aid convoys. I was responsible for everything to do with international organisations present in Srebrenica. As concerns the convoys, mostly during that period of time, immediately before the attack on Srebrenica, convoys for the Dutch and for the Muslim civilians coming in were prevented from entering. The Bratunac Brigade had no authority to keep convoys out or let them in. All orders that were issued in this respect went from the main staff through the Drina Corps command, through the Bratunac Brigade, trickling down to us eventually. We were the last to receive these orders, and we had the task to stop certain convoys, to reduce the number of trucks in a convoy, or to make certain requests regarding the humanitarian aid being shipped into Srebrenica. As for the Dutch Battalion, the situation was perfectly clear. DutchBat was not allowed to have sufficient supplies of fuel, victuals, or other staples that were necessary for the proper and normal functioning of DutchBat. The final aim of these restrictions imposed against DutchBat was for DutchBat not to be ready for combat, not to be ready for carrying out their tasks within the enclave. This was the chief reason why no supplies of fuel, victuals, clothes and other staples, and other things were not allowed into the enclave. The rotation of certain units and companies was not allowed either. All these restrictive measures had the same aim as I just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was your opinion of the reason to restrict humanitarian aid to the Muslim inhabitants of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My personal opinion, and this was common knowledge, this was one of the ways to make the Muslim population leave the enclave as soon as possible. This was the final aim, the final objective, to make life unbearable for the people in the enclave. To make it impossible for them to live on, and as a consequence people would then eventually leave the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you first become aware that there was a plan to attack the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, could we break here. I think it's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And I hope during the break, during the afternoon, the court manager in your team could work with Madam Registrar for the numbers of certain documents so as to facilitate the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's my fault. I think I hid it from her by accident. But we'll sort that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 1.02 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, when did you first become aware of the plan to attack the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I first became aware of the plan in July, early July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how did you become aware of it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The then corps commander, General Zivanovic told me. He was in the Bratunac Brigade. This was no official meeting. We were sitting outside the Bratunac Brigade headquarters. We were seated at a table. And he spoke about the attack on the Srebrenica enclave. He also spoke about the intentions of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did he say about the intentions?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He said that Srebrenica should be separated from Zepa, that an attack on Srebrenica should be carried out, and that Srebrenica was to be defeated militarily and cleansed from its Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there anybody else with you and General Zivanovic when he was talking about this?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can only say that to the best of my recollection, with us at the table was also Major Trisic, 2nd Lieutenant Micic, and some other members of the brigade who just happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was this a formal announcement or an informal -- how did this come about that he just says this at a table outside the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, this was no official meeting. General Zivanovic, who hailed from the area, from Bratunac, the village of Fakovici, that is Ducici, he did not stay very often in the zone of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you again say the village that Zivanovic was from?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: General Zivanovic hailed from a village, the village of Ducici. I think this village is part of Srebrenica municipality, but I'm not positive. Geographically speaking, it might be somewhere on the border. However, the name of the village is Ducici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you become -- was there any official announcement of this attack plan after Zivanovic told you informally?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of any official announcement. I did not have an opportunity to see any official announcement. Not in the sense that I had insight into documents, the complete set of documents related to the attack. However, in my position, I knew when preparations were underway for the attack on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did the brigade start making preparations for the attack?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Preparations began much earlier, much before the official date when everything became obvious. In my estimate - this is a personal assessment I'm giving you - the preparations began when the UNPROFOR checkpoint in Zelani Jel was attacked and when this checkpoint was taken. This is late May or early June. Intensive preparations began in late June and early July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again for the record, the village of Zelani Jadar is what you said?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, the attack itself, were Bratunac Brigade forces involved in that attack?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. The battalions, or rather members of the Bratunac Brigade were involved in that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe other units that you're aware of that were involved in the attack.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, in addition to units of the Bratunac Brigade, units from the Drina Corps were also involved in the attack on Srebrenica. More specifically, a Zvornik Brigade unit usually referred to as the Drina Wolves. For the most part, those were, conditionally speaking, combat groups established in brigades that belonged to the Drina Corps. Furthermore, some units of the main staff also took part. Elements of the 65th Protection Regiment, part of the 10th Sabotage Detachment of the main staff, and elements of police forces from the special MUP brigade of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: During the time of the attack, were you aware of any targeting of civilian objects in the enclave by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What I can say is that I had no opportunity to see any plan of the artillery attack, or rather artillery fire. But I do know that the town of Srebrenica was the target of artillery fire, a target which I consider to be a civilian target.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your interview earlier with Bruce Bursik, myself, you stated that the school at Potocari and the March 11th factory were also civilian targets. Do you stand by that today?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This information was not part of the intelligence that I had. In my own assessment, at the time I classified them as civilian targets. However, based on what I saw later, when I saw the Krivaja plan, I realised that I had been wrong and those had been no civilian targets. I believe I made a mistake there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you're referring to the document entitled "the Krivaja 1995 attack plan" which was the Drina Corps plan of attack which will be the subject of a later exhibit, Your Honour. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Aside from the shelling of Srebrenica town, were you aware of any other targeting of civilians or civilian objects?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I know for sure that there was firing on, I believe, the 11th of July, 1995, in the afternoon hours when word reached me that enemy forces from the direction of Srebrenica were moving towards Potocari, and then on to Bratunac. I know for a fact that civilians were being targeted, civilians who were on the move, and those were certainly no military units travelling down that road. Concerning this same situation, following the fall of the Srebrenica enclave, and military observers confirmed this information, military observers present in Srebrenica at the time, they also told me that on that same day, civilians had been targeted along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We need to go question, question, answer by question, answer. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know what units targeted or shot at those civilians coming up from Srebrenica towards Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It could have only been from the zone of responsibility of the 2nd infantry battalion. From the so-called cockade or star region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that battalion a battalion of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the 2nd infantry battalion from the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know what sort of ammunition we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At those positions, I think there was a B1 gun, or a Zis. I think that's a 76 millimetre gun. I think that's a Z-i-s, a Zis. That would be a 76 millimetre gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that an artillery piece as opposed to a mortar, or is it a mortar? Sorry, my knowledge doesn't go too much beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It's not a mortar. My knowledge of artillery pieces is also limited, but no, it's not a mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: During this period of 11 July, where did you spend your time on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was in the zone of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade, or to be more precise, I was in the command of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what senior officers, if any, had arrived to the Bratunac Brigade either on or before the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as the presence of officers in the Bratunac Brigade is concerned, I personally saw General Mladic from the main staff. I also saw Colonel Jankovic, also from the main staff, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric from the Drina Corps command. I saw -- I would see General Krstic who at the time was the chief of staff of the Drina Corps. I would see General Zivanovic. And I also saw commanders who were the commanders of these combat groups, Commander Zekovic, chief of the 2nd Motorised Brigade. So I saw these officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did any particular -- any of these officers actually make their base in the Bratunac Brigade offices that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the main staff, the administration, Colonel Jankovic found office space in that command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you say Colonel Jankovic is from the main staff. Do you know what unit or branch he was from, what his job was?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Colonel Jankovic was part of the intelligence department. He was involved in the intelligence and security field. He was part of the intelligence administration of the main staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where in particular did he set up his office?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He had an office -- you mean in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He had an office where my office was. That was in the building where the command of the Bratunac Brigade had its offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall what day he actually moved in?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 8th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you notice any other main staff officers from the intelligence and security section arrive in the Bratunac area prior to the fall of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: From the intelligence section, no, I didn't see anyone. I didn't notice any other officers. But I heard that there was another officer who was present there. But I personally did not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about Captain Pecanac. I know he's from the intelligence sector, but I don't know what his post was in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about any officers from the security section of the main staff? Did you see them in Bratunac before the fall on 11 July?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Not before the fall of the enclave. I didn't see anyone from the main staff. I may have seen Colonel Beara, whom I know. I didn't see him, but I heard he was present in Bratunac. A day -- on the day that the enclave fell, or the day before, but I didn't see him. I heard he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What day did the enclave fall?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The enclave was taken over on the 11th. That's when it fell. And the forces of the army of Republika Srpska took it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who is Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Colonel Beara is an officer from the main staff. He was the chief of the security department in the main staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any officers from the Ministry of the Interior combat forces at around this time frame?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes, I saw members of the special brigade from the MUP, from the Ministry of the Interior, during that period. And if we're talking about the period after the enclave fell, I saw the chief of the centre of security, Colonel Vasic. The centre was the Zvornik centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's start with the special police forces. What officer or officers did you see from the special police forces in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I saw the deputy commander of the special MUP brigade of Republika Srpska, Mr. Miso Goracanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, just for the record, to get the pronunciation and the spelling right, who was the commander again?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The commander of the special MUP brigade was Mr. Goran Saric, the general, and the deputy commander of the special MUP brigade was Mr. Ljubisa Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the person who you actually saw in Bratunac was the deputy commander. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when did you the deputy commander in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Ljubisa Borovcanin on the 11th of July, 1995, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what the minister of the interior special police forces are, how they are different from the army of the Republika Srpska combat forces?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll first of all try to explain, or rather to tell you that in terms of combat capacities, the structure, the organisation, I think these units were very similar to the units of the Republika Srpska Army. They're organised in the same way as the units of the Republika Srpska Army, into platoons and companies. And instead of battalions, the special MUP brigade had its detachments. There were a number of them. I don't know how many of them they had, but they had a number of detachments within that brigade. They had automatic and semiautomatic weapons, just like the members of the Republika Srpska Army. They had armoured mechanised vehicles, tanks, armoured personnel carriers, Pragas, and other heavy weapons. So the special MUP brigade was a combat unit from the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This weapon, the Praga, will come up perhaps again. Can you explain to us briefly what a Praga is.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It's a self-propelled device. I don't know what kind of weapon it is exactly. I think it has a 12.7 millimetre machine-gun, perhaps guns of other calibres, too. A Praga is a weapon that has guns that uses ammunition of a large calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there other minister of interior forces that could be used as combat forces in the area of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the area of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All throughout Bosnia actually, aside from the special police forces, were there other Ministry of the Interior combat units?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the nature of the question. He's talking about the entire country of Bosnia. I thought we were discussing Srebrenica at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Would you please focus your question on certain areas. Or you may tell us the reason why you asked that broad question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, these fundamental structures that I'm going through are applicable for the entire region of Bosnia. And I was just trying to clarify the question for the witness so he understood what I was getting at. And I'm not interested in these forces working outside of the area we're concerned, so I don't intend to go into that. I'll just ask him a few more questions on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please concentrate on the area which is relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you aware of police -- other police forces that were -- that would be engaged in combat in the Zvornik/Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of the fact that there were special-purposes police units from the Ministry of the Interior that were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe what those forces are as opposed to the forces under Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I should tell the Court, there's a translation issue with these forces. They both get translated as "special" in English, but it's a different word in Bosnian. But I think it will be made clear that we're talking about distinct forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So could you explain the difference between the forces you just mentioned and the forces under the command of Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The forces that were under the command of Ljubisa Borovcanin were units of the special brigade. And the PUP units were units which were formed at the level of a centre. And I know that the Zvornik centre had such units that had been established. The main difference between the special MUP brigade and the PUP units, the PJP units were mainly composed of men from the territory where that unit was formed. Up to 80 or 90 per cent of the men came from the territory where that unit was formed. So a company was formed for the Bratunac area. For such a company from the SJB, the public security station, you would appoint a commander, and it would be brought up to strength with men on the whole who were from that area. And as far as weapons are concerned, those units didn't possess heavy weapons. They had infantry weapons, automatic, and semi-automatic weapons. On the whole, they didn't have Pragas, they didn't have tanks, and they didn't have other heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you met Mr. Borovcanin on the afternoon of the 11th of July, can you tell us what occurred.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I met him in the afternoon. He was in the Zuti Most area. I was called to come, summoned to the Zuti Most area, and Ljubisa Borovcanin asked me to show him the military objectives, the fortified features and the trenches in the area of the village of Budak and the village of Likavi [phoen]. As an intelligence officer, it was my duty to know about these things, and I showed these military objectives to Ljubisa Borovcanin. He fired at these objectives from a T-55 tank in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell what kind of forces he had with him at that time? Numbers of people? Equipment?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On the whole, what I was able to see, the young members of that special MUP brigade, he had automatic weapons, mostly automatic weapons, a tank at Zuti Most when I was there. And I couldn't tell you what the strength was exactly, the strength of the forces. Perhaps between 200, 250, maybe 300 men. I really couldn't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how did you happen to meet with him that afternoon? Had you received any prior information about his arrival in the area?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. The first time I saw him and heard that he had come was when I was summoned to the Zuti Most. I hadn't been informed that he was coming on that day. I previously heard that he was supposed to come, but I didn't know exactly on what date or at what time he was supposed to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How did you hear that Borovcanin was supposed to come to the area?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time, I had contact with the chief of the SJB from Bratunac, Mr. Josipovic, and he told me that they were expecting parts of the special brigade to arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why were they arriving, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They came to help, to step up combat operations because as far as I know, they were expecting the Muslim forces to put up fierce resistance. And as far as I know, no one thought that the resistance would be so short lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you do after assisting Mr. Borovcanin and his forces?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After that, I returned to the Bratunac Brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know roughly what time you arrived there on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think it was about 1800 hours, but I really can't remember exactly now. It was before night had come. It was about 1800 hours, perhaps, 1830 hours. 1900 hours. I really don't know exactly. That's when I returned to the brigade. Perhaps it was a little earlier. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of any meeting or meetings that occurred between superior officers at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters in the evening hours after you returned?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When I returned to the brigade command, all I knew was that a meeting was supposed to be held in the Fontana Hotel in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, I will get to that meeting. But were you aware of any meetings of VRS officers at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters on the evening of the 11th or the evening of the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm in a little -- in a slight dilemma. I know that one of the meetings was held in the evening. I'm not sure whether it was on the 11th or on the 12th. And I can't answer your question precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. But tell us what you can remember. How do you know there was a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was on the 11th or 12th, but I know that a meeting was held in the Bratunac Brigade command in the evening. And it was attended by commanders of those combat groups, together with the chief of staff, General Krstic, who was in charge of the operations. And I know that that meeting was held in the office of Commander Blagojevic. But I really don't know whether it was on the 11th or on the 12th. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know whether Commander Blagojevic was part of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say the commanders of the combat groups, is that the groups that you've mentioned earlier that were involved in the attack on the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Colonel Andric, Vinko Pandurevic. From the 2nd Romanija Brigade, I don't know what the officer's name was. But these officers participated in the attack on Srebrenica and were in command of those groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So were you present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who did you hear about it from?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This is something that I saw. I saw the commanders who came to the barracks. I saw them entering and leaving that office. And after that meeting, I found out about certain things, so I was able to come to the conclusion that it was a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, tell us who you found out information about that meeting from.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You mean when the meeting in the Bratunac Brigade command would be held? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You just made reference that you had found out certain things about that meeting, and I'm just asking you who you heard about the meeting from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, the witness said he saw those participants coming in and out of the meeting. And then later on, he found out about certain things. So he was able to come to the conclusion there was a meeting. It's quite clear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just was asking about who he found those certain things from, is what I meant to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't found out about it from anyone in particular. No one told me that there was a meeting in the Bratunac Brigade. No one told me about the people attending the people. Everything that I have said, these are things that I saw because I was present in the Bratunac Brigade command. And I saw all of this. But after that meeting, I heard something that just confirmed the fact that this meeting had been held. They discussed preparing forces for Zepa. Vinko Pandurevic objected to this. It's quite natural that I was able to draw this conclusion. And that is what I can remember as far as this meeting is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember who told you the details about the meeting that you just mentioned, about Mr. Pandurevic objecting to going to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think that afterwards, this was discussed in the brigade command. And Colonel Blagojevic spoke about this, too, and about certain other details from that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what else you remember that Colonel Blagojevic said about this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think they discussed the fact that General Krstic was unhappy about the action of Bratunac units, from the Bratunac Brigade. Something like that. But they really didn't discuss any particular details. They just mentioned what the forthcoming orders would be, and they discussed the activities of the Bratunac Brigade units and how they should be viewed. That's what I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From your position, what was the role of General Zivanovic and the role of General Krstic in the attack of the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In my view, General Zivanovic was officially the corps commander. Yet again, General Krstic in my personal opinion was the man who really ran the operation and called all the shots. That's my personal take on it as far as those two generals are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's go back to where we know we are on 11 July. And you mentioned that you had found out about a meeting at the Hotel Fontana. Can you tell us how you found out about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When I returned from Zuti Most, Colonel Jankovic informed me that on the 11th of July, there would be a meeting at the Fontana Hotel, a meeting with General Mladic and representatives of DutchBat in attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you have any responsibilities relating to that, or were you given any by anyone?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Jankovic told me that I should provide security -- that I should make sure an interpreter was present, and that I should arrange security for the hotel during the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you have any information whether or not your commander Blagojevic was aware of the instructions that Jankovic had given you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I didn't report this to Commander Blagojevic at the time, and I really don't know whether he had information that this meeting would take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why didn't you inform your commander of your job to provide security for the meeting at Fontana?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The reason was that there were certain tasks that were within the purview of the intelligence and security organ. There would have been no need to do that. Those were day-to-day tasks. There would have been no need for me to run over to Commander Blagojevic and inform him about everything single thing that I had to do. Those were my day-to-day tasks, my regular tasks. I did not need to obtain special authorisation from Commander Blagojevic in order to carry out those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was a -- how was General Mladic and DutchBat a day-to-day task? To an outsider, that seems like something that is not an everyday occurrence. How was it that you viewed that as an everyday task?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You are right, counsel. This was no day-to-day task. If you had the commander of the main staff present in the zone, that certainly would have been no day-to-day task. But I knew my duties, what my duties would be if he were present in Bratunac. I knew what to do in terms of securing the building, the premises where he was to hold a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After I received my task, I made sure the interpreter, Petar Uscumlic was at the hotel. I used my police contacts to bring him. 30 minutes later perhaps, I went to the Hotel Fontana myself, and I took all the relevant measures, starting with physical security and ranging to evacuating the hotel in order for the hotel to be prepared for that meeting to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did your work in this regard involve communicating with the military police platoon of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain when you first communicated with them and how that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, I asked the military police commander, Mirko Jankovic, to give me a sufficient number of men to provide security for the Fontana Hotel, which he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many men did he give you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think there were five or six people for security. In addition to those, I'm not counting in one department of the Bratunac Brigade military police, that was always providing security. But that's escorting General Mladic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you need to get approval of your commander Blagojevic before requesting troops from Mirko Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That was not normal procedure. In order to carry out this police task to provide security - personal security - for anyone in particular, I would not have needed to ask for authorisation. This was an everyday task. It was a very usual police task, usual for the police and for me as the chief of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you describe the events as you brought the interpreter to the meeting and what do you recall happening as people arrived.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Briefly, yes. Fontana Hotel was prepared for the meeting. It had been evacuated and empty as a result. A room was envisaged to have the meeting in, and we waited for General Mladic's arrival. At the hotel, he would arrive with his colleagues and with representatives of DutchBat. At first, we were standing near the entrance, Petar Uscumlic , the interpreter, and myself. After a while, we were joined by Colonel Jankovic. General Mladic arrived with the people escorting him. His security entered the hall, and he followed. General Zivanovic was with him. I welcomed him. So did Colonel Jankovic and Petar. We introduced our interpreter to them, and the interpreter said his last name was Uscumlic. General Zivanovic then started yelling and he threw the interpreter out of the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was General Zivanovic or General Mladic that started yelling?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: General Mladic. I apologise. Did I say Zivanovic? General Mladic was the one who started yelling. The reason he had thrown the interpreter out of the room is because he was convinced that the interpreter was a Muslim. He proceeded to the room, the hall, where the meeting was to be held. He was followed by people from DutchBat, Mr. Karremans and his two colleagues, who were officers. Colonel Jankovic took over the role of interpreter. He spoke some English. That proved a failure. Then I was ordered. I was standing a stone's throw away from that room. I was ordered to find someone else to interpret. Someone told him it was Petar Uscumlic. And I went outside and brought Petar back into the room, and that's when Petar became the interpreter. And he was to serve as our interpreter for all the meetings that later took place at the Fontana Hotel. This first meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me ask you, do you know where your commander Blagojevic was at the time this first meeting was underway?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Really, I didn't see Colonel Blagojevic at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters at that time, or rather I didn't go to his office, to the section of the building where his office was. I can't tell you if he was there. I assume he might have been at that time. But I really can't say. I don't know whether he was or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there any other representative of the Bratunac Brigade at that first meeting besides yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection to the characterisation representative. The gentleman has never indicated he was there representing the Bratunac Brigade. He was ordered by the main staff to provide certain services without the knowledge or the authorisation of his commander. So I object strenuously to the word "representative."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you may use other words. Maybe "were there any other people from the brigade at that first meeting?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there in other people from the Bratunac Brigade at that first meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, no, not to my knowledge. There was no one else there at that first meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why were you the only one there as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was at the meeting as the chief of the security and intelligence organ which had the role that I have already explained, to do with preparations providing security for the commander of the main staff and all the other persons attending the meeting. As for the participation of DutchBat, I was also the liaison officer for the needs of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you there under your normal military -- performing your normal military duties as the chief of security and intelligence for the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And under whose authority are you acting when you're performing your normal duties under the -- as the chief of security and intelligence of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, as always under the authority of the unit commander, which is only logical. I never do anything on my own behalf. I do what I'm supposed to do as part of my remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then did Colonel Jankovic's instructions to you appear in any way to be part of some secret that was being kept from the command of the Bratunac Brigade? Was there anything secret that was being kept from the Bratunac Brigade that occurred at the Hotel Fontana as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object to this line of questioning. First of all, it's a mischaracterisation. The objection that was raised has nothing to do with secrecy. It has to do whether he was there as an official representative of the Bratunac Brigade. He has indicated that he never went to Colonel Blagojevic's commander after receiving the order from Colonel Jankovic because he wasn't there, that is, Colonel Blagojevic wasn't there. So now the Prosecutor wishes to inject the word "secrecy" as if there was some sort of secret operation. I think he can rephrase the question. But as it's phrased, I believe it's misleading, it's a mischaracterisation, and I believe it's prejudicial in the way it's phrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, maybe you can put your question in some other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm just looking for the jury. I don't see one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this kind of behaviour. These are theatrics, and he's behaving like a drama queen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, can you tell us -- were you able to see the video in the Prosecution's possession of the first meeting at the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you cannot be seen on that video, can you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you were during that first meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, we lost the answer of the witness in the transcript. You asked, "you can't be seen on that video, can you?" Then we missed. Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you be seen on the video of that first meeting of the -- at the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you were during the first meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I was not in the room where the commander General Ratko Mladic and representatives of DutchBat alongside with the interpreter Uscumlic, Petar were. I was outside the room standing at a distance of between 3 and 5 metres from the scene actually being recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why were you out in the wings like that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Because I was doing my job. In my capacity as chief of security, in such circumstances, I chose my own spot where I thought I should stand, where I should position myself. In the room or outside or anywhere else where the meeting was being held for that matter. I could see everything that was going on and everything that was being said from where I decided to position myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you give us, briefly, just your impressions of what went on at that first meeting.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, my impression, my assessment is that this was no meeting at all. All those who were present were standing. General Mladic was the only speaker. He was trying to intimidate the DutchBat commander and his officers. He was threatening them. And he was acting violently. He dictated his terms, told them what he wanted to say. The tone was that of an order, and no one except Mladic said anything at that meeting. He asked the questions and provided the answers. This was all finished in no time at all. An ultimatum was given to the DutchBat commander as to what he should do before the next meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The request was for the DutchBat commander by 11.00 the same evening to get representatives of the Muslim armed forces, Muslim representatives, and reappear with them for a second meeting the same evening. Which, of course, Mr. Karremans said he would see what he could do about it. And then he went back with his colleagues, back to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you receive any instructions from anyone?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After that meeting, I knew there would be the next meeting, at about 11.00. And no one gave me any special instructions. I knew what I was supposed to do for that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So was there a second meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was held sometime between 10.00 and 11.00 the same evening. I think it was almost 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you do during that period, from the end of the first meeting and the beginning of the second meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I went over to my office at the Bratunac Brigade command, and I wrote up a report including all the information I received on the 11th from the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had you received any information at that time about the number of people around Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received information mostly from the 2nd Infantry Battalion concerning a large number of civilians moving towards the UN base in Potocari. I received information also that there were between one and two thousand military-aged men among those civilians moving towards the UN base. That was the information I received then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you communicate that information about the one to two thousand military-aged men in Potocari to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I conveyed this information to the command, which means that the information had previously reached the operations duty officer. My opinion is that those who were in command of the Bratunac Brigade had been informed in the same way. All the officers who would have found the information relevant could have obtained it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe that process by where information comes into the duty officer and that others would become aware of it, other commanders -- excuse me, other officers of the -- in the command. How does that work?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the information being passed on to the operations room, I'm talking about intelligence, this information is mostly meant for the command of the Bratunac Brigade. First of all, the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, chief of staff, and the other high-ranking commanders. The direct way to convey information is not the only way to inform the superior commanders. The operations room and the operations duty officer, at any time the information is received in the operations room, must inform the superior officer, the commander, if we are dealing with the kind of information that cannot wait, no matter where the commander happens to be at the time. In his office or somewhere with his subordinate units, the 1st, 2nd, 3rd infantry battalion. This didn't matter. That's how it worked in units, the level of brigade. That's how it works. There are a number of other ways to convey information, but this is the method we used in our brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you receive any intelligence that these able-bodied men were armed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. I did not have information that those people in that group moving towards Potocari were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you pass on the information about the able-bodied men in written form or in oral form to anyone after you received it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I passed on the information in writing to my superior command, the Drina Corps command, security and intelligence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you discuss this information orally with anyone?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I discussed this with the operations duty officer at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters or command building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall who that was on this night of the 11th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember the person's name. But I do know that there was information coming from the security and intelligence organs and from the commanders of subordinate units, and that both streams of information were almost identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did your duty officer office have a logbook where this kind of information was noted down in?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, mostly. There was an operations duty logbook where the operations duty officer would enter all the information and all the changes, all the requests, all the orders, anything that happened during his time on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you pass on this information about the numbers of able-bodied men to any of the -- any senior officers from the corps or in the main staff that night?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As I said, I wrote up a report that I forwarded to the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Orally, did you contact any of the people that had been at the Hotel Fontana about this information?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in touch with Colonel Jankovic, who was with me all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see it's 2.15. It's a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nikolic, now you are a witness under oath in this case. So during the break, do not talk to anybody about your testimony, and do not let anybody talk to you about it. You may consult with your counsel on the legal issues, but not on the factual issues. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Clear enough, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll resume next Monday morning, 9.00, in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: at 2.17 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 22nd day of September, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 25
